sections.html:
• Name: Chinese mitten crab
  • Other names: Chinese freshwater edible crab, Shanghai crab, Chinese river crab
  • Scientific name: Eriocheir sinensis
  • Minimum tank size: ~60 litres
  • Type: Freshwater
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Average carapace size: 7–8 cm
  • Average leg span: about 18–20 cm
  • Diet: Mostly herbivore/omnivore
  • Temperament: Aggressive
  • Colour: Brown

Eriocheir sinensis is a very successful invasive crab species in Europe and has been nominated as one of 100 of the "World's Worst" invaders. Even if it is not banned in your state or country, NEVER release them into the wild! These crabs can alter ecosystems, causing the loss of native species and having major economic consequences.

The mitten crab is a traditional and common savory food in China due to its delicious taste and high nutritional value.

The Chinese mitten crab is a native of East Asia. Its native range extends from Hong Kong to the border with North Korea.

In 1912, these crabs were introduced into Germany. Since then, they have spread throughout northern Europe. Their estimated distribution now ranges from Finland, through Sweden, Russia, Poland, Germany, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Belgium and England to France.

They are also found in San Francisco Bay, Chesapeake Bay and the mid-Atlantic coast of North America, where the species has become one of the most notorious aquatic invaders.

The Chinese mitten crabs inhabit rivers, streams, creeks, marshes, lakes, as well as estuaries and intertidal areas from lower shorelines to about 10 m in depth.

This species has no preference and can be found in rocky, muddy and vegetated areas.

Adults live predominantly in freshwater but migrate seawards to breed.

Keep the Chinese mitten crab in a large tank because of its growth potential. This species is also very active and needs a lot of space.

A tank of about 60 litres is the minimum recommended size.

As adults, one male and one female may be kept together in an enclosure of 180 litres or more, but two adult males would need far more space to reduce territorial fighting.

  • A smaller tank will significantly limit their freedom and make them more aggressive towards each other. Eventually it will stress them and reduce their lifespan.
  • They are very good escape artists, so tanks should be covered. They are also strong and can move light lids.

Chinese mitten crabs are very adaptable and can thrive in most situations, so care is quite simple. Still, their core needs should be addressed.

If you are a first-time crab owner, cycle your tank before bringing any pet home. Once the tank is cycled, check water quality with a test kit.

Crabs are slow eaters, so food can be left for 24 hours before removal. Do not leave uneaten food for too long, as it can cause smell and bacteria; these crabs like to store uneaten food in their burrows.

Decorations and hiding spots

They appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, wood, plants, PVC pipes and other decorations. Shelter significantly reduces the rate of aggressive behaviour. Plenty of hiding places also minimise stress and are critical for molting.

Molting

Because crabs have an exoskeleton, they must molt to grow. It also allows them to restore lost limbs. The process consists of 4 phases: pre-molt, molt, post-molt and inter-molt.

  • NEVER disturb crabs about to molt. Do not panic if you do not see them for a few days. This is the most stressful moment in their life.
  • Keep putting and replacing food in the tank.
  • Keep giving calcium-rich food.
  • Do not remove the old exoskeleton from the tank. It contains lots of minerals and the crabs will eat it later.

Handling rules

  • They are not pets to play with. Do not take them out just because you want to.
  • Never lift them by their legs or claws. They can lose a limb by autotomy.
  • Provide as many hiding places as you can.
  • Make sure the lid is closed tightly so they cannot escape.

• Temperature: preferred 15–21°C, considered optimal. The species tolerates a wide range; growth ceases only below 7°C and above 30°C.
  • pH: 7.0–8.5
  • Hardness: KH 3–20, GH 3–25
  • Salinity: adults are extremely euryhaline and can quickly adapt from highly saline to low brackish and freshwater environments.

Adults are also highly tolerant of desiccation and can remain unsubmerged for several hours without mortality.

Filtration: Sponge filters are a bad idea, as the crabs will chip, chew and break apart the sponge. Use filtration that cannot be easily damaged, for example hang-on-back or canister filters.

Lighting: No special requirements.

Substrate: Small gravel and/or sand substrates are ideal.

Chinese mitten crabs are predominantly omnivorous and detritivorous feeders and will eat whatever they can get. Gut content analysis showed they feed on aquatic plants, algae, detritus, fish eggs, insects and small invertebrates. They become more carnivorous as they age.

Suggested foods in aquariums:

  • Vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumbers, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • Fruits (sweet apple, banana, pear, melon, mango, etc.)
  • Leaves
  • Shrimp pellets and granules
  • Fish food (TetraMin flakes, etc.)
  • Shrimp food (Hikari Shrimp Cuisine, algae wafers, etc.)
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms

Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week for adults, daily for juveniles. Do not let them starve or they can start cannibalizing very fast.

Calcium

Calcium is a crucial component of the exoskeleton and overall health. Sources include kale, broccoli, spinach, cuttlebones, dusted eggshells, figs, nuts, oyster shells, seaweed, seeds and insects. Keep a small piece of cuttlefish bone in the enclosure at all times.

Although fully aquatic, Chinese mitten crabs can cross dry land to enter new river systems. They are extremely active during the day and far less active at night.

They are burrowers and in nature can cause serious river bank erosion. However, it is mostly the smaller juveniles (up to 2.5–3 cm carapace length) that construct and inhabit burrows (up to 50 cm deep).

They are aggressive and territorial. Males show a significantly higher rate of aggression than females. Aggression can decline with greater availability of shelter and food.

  • Social: No
  • Active: Yes
  • Peaceful: No
  • Territorial: Yes
  • Burrowers: Yes

Tankmates

It can be risky to house multiple animals together, especially males. They should not be kept with crabs, crayfish, dwarf frogs and especially freshwater snails, which they consume voraciously.

They usually do not hunt fish, but bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (like Betta) should be avoided. The chance of these relatively slow crabs capturing healthy free-swimming fish is low.

Dwarf shrimp are too small and fast, but the crabs are opportunistic, so you may still lose shrimp from time to time. Ideally, keep them alone.

Plants

They are not plant safe. They will eat, cut, shred or uproot plants, so planted tanks are not recommended. Viable options are plastic plants, floating plants and cheap plants you are ready to lose.

The species is sexually dimorphic.

  • Size: Females are generally smaller than males.
  • Setae: Both sexes have hairy chelae, but the setae are generally fuller and cover a wider area in males.
  • Abdomen: Once the carapace width exceeds about 2.5 cm, the sexes can be distinguished by abdomen shape. Males have a narrow, slimmer (triangular) plate, while females have a broad plate on the belly.

The Chinese mitten crab has a catadromous life cycle: adult stage in freshwater, reproduction in brackish water, and a marine larval stage. Crabs mature at about 3.5 cm carapace width, at 1–3 years in China and 3–5 years in Europe.

The species generally reproduces only once or rarely twice, and then both sexes die: males after mating, females after the eggs hatch.

Eggs

After mating in the brackish water of estuaries, females move toward higher salinities and release larvae in early spring. A single mating can allow up to 2 spawnings. Females can carry 250,000 to 1,000,000 eggs in the first spawn. The second maturation occurs about a month after the first spawn, much shorter than the first maturation (3–4 months). Eggs are carried attached to the pleopods on the underside of the abdomen.

Hatching

Fertilised eggs take 3 weeks to develop into zoeal larvae at 15–21°C and suitable salinity (20–25‰). Before hatching, the eggs turn greyish and developed eye spots can be seen.

Larvae

Larval development includes 5 zoeal stages and one megalopa stage, lasting 2–4 days per zoeal stage and 5–10 days for the megalopa, depending on temperature, food and salinity. Start water changes after the first 3 days of culture: 10–20% (2nd and 3rd stage), 40–50% (4th and 5th stage), and 100% at the end of the rearing cycle.

Larvae can develop through metamorphosis at 12–18°C and salinities of 15 to 32‰. Even under optimal conditions, survival from first stage to megalopa is usually about 10–15%.

Larvae feed primarily on microalgae, phytoplankton, rotifers, copepods and artemia. Cannibalism often occurs at metamorphosis from stage 5 to megalopa, but can be reduced by increasing the feeding ration and optimising the feeding regime.

In nature, the megalopa settles in brackish water in late spring and moves upstream with tidal currents at 8–12 km per day. After 7–10 days it transforms into juveniles that migrate upstream (1–3 km per day) into freshwater, reaching rivers, lakes and ponds as far as 1200 km from the coast while growing to adult size.

The adult carapace averages 7–8 cm long, with a leg span up to 18–20 cm or more. Adults can weigh 250–300 grams. Coloration varies from brownish-orange (mostly juveniles) to greenish-brown in adults and newly molted crabs.

Distinguishing characteristics:

  • Dense patches of setae (hair) on the white-tipped claws, which give the crab its name as they resemble mittens.
  • 4 lateral spines on either side of the eyes.
  • A distinctive notch between the eyes.
  • The carapace is slightly wider than long.

Lifespan depends on maturity and breeding, as the crabs die soon after. Normal lifespan varies from 1–3 years in China to 3–5 years in Europe.
